utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning to the technical booth, to the interpreters. Yes, I can hear you. We're back to resume the case against General Krstic. I believe I see Mr. Cayley behind this pillar. There's always this problem, but I see that the team is here. We can now move on with our case. I believe we have one witness today. Mr. Harmon, is that so?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We are continuing with Mrs. Omanovic, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours; good morning, counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mrs. Omanovic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You will now resume your evidence today. I should like to remind you that you are still under your solemn declaration, and you will continue to answer questions which Mr. Harmon will ask of you. Thank you. Examined by Mr. Harmon: [Cont'd]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Omanovic.

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we return to your description of the events in Potocari, I want to ask you a few questions about some individuals. Do you know the Streten Petrovic family?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, that family, because Streten lived in the same area with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Approximately how old is Streten Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forty-ish. Slightly younger than I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of Streten Petrovic's father?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They called him Ilija Saspata, and even before the war he had a very characteristic long moustache.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, let us return to where we were yesterday when we took a recess. In your testimony, you had described your flight from Srebrenica to Potocari, and you told us that you had arrived at a location known as the Zinc Factory. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We reached the compound of the zinc plating unit and that is where we spent the night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Judges the conditions in which you found yourself at the zinc factory?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived from Srebrenica, we were in the yard of the zinc factory and nearby factories. People came there simply -- I don't know why, but we somehow thought we would not go any further because the UN base was there. So we somehow thought we should put up there for the night, that we should make the best we could. And everybody, whatever personal effects he had with him, looked where he would spend the night. So it was kind of a plateau, an area where we gathered. I found a cover of a container that they used to zinc plate in that factory, so we used that, covered it, and that was our bed. The baby had its pram, and we left our belongings in the pram and we simply lied down on the ground. Or, rather, you couldn't lay down, you simply had a corner where you waited what would happen next. As we sat there, snipers would fire every now and then, and all this throng would then move to one side or the other, screaming. Above us was the Pecista village where the Serb soldiers were firing at houses. The sound of that shell, again we would simply dodge to one side or the other with frightened cries, and that is how we spent the night. Some were throwing up, some were scared. It was the area where you lived, even the -- that area, that small tight space was everything to us, the bedroom, the bathroom, everything. We were simply all crowded there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the village of Pecista. Could you tell the Judges what you saw happening to that particular village and houses around it?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Above the village of Pecista, along the edges of the village, the houses were -- around there the houses were torched. They were firing shells and everything was going up in the air.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in a position where you could see the soldiers lighting the houses on fire?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't see the soldiers myself, but the houses were being put on fire. You can't see it with the naked eye but you can see the flames. You can see it's burning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in and around the zinc factory, how many people were with you? Can you estimate the number of refugees?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exact number I couldn't really give you, but there were some several thousand people in that area. We were packed close together, and the area couldn't have had more than one kilometre square, and yet all people who had arrived from Srebrenica were there in all those production plants around the zinc plating factory. The 11 of March, the zinc plating unit, and down to the yellow ribbon that separated the UN base from the rest of the world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kind of food, what kind of water was available to the refugees?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only what one happened to bring along, but mostly people went without food and without water.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President and Your Honours, I'm going to now show a film clip that is approximately 47 seconds long, so it is a clip that will be -- you have to look at very quickly, but it will show the crowds of people. If we could have the lights reduced and we could show this clip. As I say, it's very brief, and it's taken from footage that we have available to us, and we believe it accurately reflects the number of people in and around at the particular moment. It is Exhibit number 51.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Omanovic, you've seen this film footage before, because I've shown it to you, but does this accurately show in some respects the number of people, refugees who were in and around the buildings in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite, as this film shows. It describes accurately the situation in which we found ourselves in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the night of the 11th, when you were in and around the Zinc Factory, can you tell the Judges the general mood, the general mental state of the refugees?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were all frightened, people were all hungry, people were scared out of their wits. They didn't know what would happen next, so that those were people who were terrified. I don't know -- I don't really know how to describe it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's focus our attention, then, on the following day, Mrs. Omanovic, because the next day you were selected to become a representative of the Muslim people and you were selected to attend the meeting at the Hotel Fontana. Can you tell the Judges how it was that you were selected?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning, when the next morning came, Ibro Nuhanovic, Zina Civic, and Nesib Mandzic came to look for me. And they said, "We have to go to the Dutch camp to talk about putting some order in this area where we are." I was lying down on the ground and I looked very untidy, so I said, "I have to change slightly and put myself in order. Why me?" "Well," they said, "you come from Srebrenica. Most -- indigenous Srebrenica." People had left Srebrenica before the war and there were very few literate indigenous Srebrenica people left. So they chose me, as a mother, as a woman, and a literate person; they asked me to go there as a representative of women, to go to the Dutch camp to talk to them, to ask for some relief in food, an organisation there. Because the weather was so hot that after a day or two we would have certainly fallen ill from one disease or another, because it was so hot. And we would have perished simply from the heat, from diseases, from hunger, from thirst, from that disorderly life. So I went with them to the Dutch camp to talk to people so that we could organise ourselves, with their help, and try to see how to make our life more organised in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President and Your Honours, I'm going to now show you Prosecutor's Exhibit 49, which is a small segment of film footage from that meeting. The film is approximately eight minutes long. It only represents a part of the meeting. And I would ask Mr. Dubuisson to please disseminate to Your Honours copies of the transcript from that meeting. The film is Prosecutor's Exhibit 49 and the transcripts are 49A in English, 49B in French, and 49C in B/C/S. And I would ask the interpreters to please translate the film as it's being shown. Now, if we could dim the lights, please, and we could start with Prosecutor's Exhibit 49, please. Could the lights be dimmed, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "SOLDIER: This is their interpreter. "CAMILA: We are representatives -- wait a moment. "VOICE: Good morning. "NUHANOVIC: Ibro Nuhanovic. "MLADIC: What will you have? I will have mineral water, and offer them some juices. Madam, what is your profession? "CAMILA: I am an economist. "MLADIC: Where did you study? "CAMILA: In Brcko. "MLADIC: Are you married? "CAMILA: I am. "MLADIC: And your name is Amela? "CAMILA: No. Camila. "MLADIC: Camila? "CAMILA: No. Camila. I have two children and I have a grandchild. "MLADIC: Well, you are so young, and a grandmother already? "CAMILA: A grandmother. "MLADIC: When were you born? "CAMILA: 1953. "MLADIC: What did you do before? "CAMILA: I was with my colleague here in the secondary school. "MLADIC: Then you don't need me? "CAMILA: No, I don't. "MLADIC: Can you perhaps resolve the problem? You say you were schoolfellows in the same classroom, weren't you? "CAMILA: Why couldn't we? "MLADIC: Was he perhaps popular? "CAMILA: No. We were simply good friends. We didn't know that this would happen. And I mean, had we been politicians, but we were simply citizens. I never had an argument with anyone in Srebrenica, never with anyone. I just live my good solid life, my life, and it just happened so that I stayed in Srebrenica without some [indiscernible]. Here, again, what will be next? "MLADIC: Did you play any part in politics? "CAMILA: No. I was only the chief bookkeeper. I was never involved in politics. "MLADIC: And now in the war? "CAMILA: Not even in the war. "MLADIC: And the gentleman next to you? "NUHANOVIC: I'm Ibro Nuhanovic. I'm an economist, a former businessman. Now I'm in the war. Now I'm here in Srebrenica. We're stuck here. "MLADIC: Will you speak a little louder please, if you can? "NUHANOVIC: Well, I'm saying we simply happened to arrive in Srebrenica during the war. Otherwise I lived in Vlasenica. "MLADIC: And where were you born? "NUHANOVIC: I was born in the village of Soboranj, Han Pijesak municipality. "MLADIC: The village? "NUHANOVIC: Soboranj. "MLADIC: Soboran. "NUHANOVIC: I left in 1955. I went to the secondary school and then I worked here in Bratunac. I worked in Srebrenica. But they chose me to come here with these people. They invited me. "MLADIC: I want to help you but I want absolute cooperation of the civilian population. Because your army has suffered defeat, there is no need for your men to get killed; your husband, your brothers or your neighbours. All you have to do is to say what you want. And I told that to a gentleman last night. You can either survive or vanish. For your survival, I request that all your men who carry weapons, who attacked and committed crimes, the men who did commit the crimes against your people, did they hand over their weapons to the Army of Republika Srpska. And after you lay down your weapons, you can choose to either stay in the territory or, if that would suit you better, to go where you wish. The wish of every individual inhabitant here will be respected no matter how many of you there are. "CAMILA: How do we get in touch with them? "MLADIC: You are in a position to know. The rest of the army can be disarmed and lay down their weapons before my officers in the presence of UNPROFOR officers. You can choose to stay or leave if you wish. If you want to leave, you can say so and you can go to the four corners of the world. After the weapons are laid down, every individual can go where he says he wants to go. That is why it is necessary to provide the fuel. I'll provide vehicles. You can provide the fuel. You can pay for it. If you cannot afford to pay for it, then UNPROFOR should bring in four or five tanker trucks to fill up the trucks, because there are a lot of people, and that should be solved. If you choose to leave, and I do not want to influence you in any way, I have nothing against you, I have nothing against the innocent and guiltless. You can choose if you want to go east across Serbia or -- I don't mind. If you want to go west, you can say where you want to go. "VOICE: They say they want to go to Bratunac, to the stadium. "MLADIC: Right. Who said that? "VOICE: The people. "MLADIC: Are they coming here? Let them go to the stadium and one of their representatives from here will be with those people there to see them board on. "CAMILA: Could I ask you if my daughter and her child could go? "MLADIC: Well, yes. "CAMILA: She shouldn't leave her here. I'd rather stay here myself. "MLADIC: If necessary, madam, you and your daughter and granddaughter will be transferred in my vehicle. Don't worry."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Omanovic, that film clip is only a portion of the meeting; is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It is only a fragment of the meeting at which I was present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Describe the meeting, when you came in, what happened once you came in.

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I entered the room, and that is when I saw my schoolfellow Miroslav Deronjic. I was really terrified. Then at some point I turned to him and I said, "Miroslav, dear, what are you doing to all those people. Help us. They're all bare handed, hungry, barefoot, driven to the stadium like cattle, left at the mercy of those men. They're firing, targeting at them." Then Mr. Mladic told us to sit down, because we knew one another. And he said that he had experienced the greatest success of his life during those days, the conquest of Srebrenica. And my feeling was that he had prepared it all as a form of theatre, as a stage to show it all to us. He just indicated to somebody with his hand to bring something, and he brought a broken vase from the municipal hall in Srebrenica, and he said, "This is my trophy, the greatest moment in my life, the conquest of Srebrenica. I know how many people were born there." And they brought the Registry of Births, and then they brought in the Registry of Deaths and the Registry of Marriages, and he said, "I know the last person who had got married in Srebrenica." He said, "You can go anywhere you want or you can stay here or just vanish." Then I knew that if we agreed to leave there, then perhaps we might survive, and if we tried to stay, that we would simply exist no more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned at the beginning of the meeting that you had a conversation with Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have the next exhibit which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 52 disseminate, and if I could have it also placed on the ELMO. Just a little lower, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Omanovic, this is a still image taken from the film we just saw, and let me ask you if you can identify in Prosecutor's Exhibit 52 Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was sitting across the table. This is him [indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The record should reflect --

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The man with whom I went to school.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The record should reflect that Mrs. Omanovic has pointed to the man in the far right-hand corner of the image, the man in the black jacket holding a glass in his left hand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that you made a request at the beginning of the meeting or a plea of some sort to Mr. Deronjic. What did Mr. Deronjic say to you after you made that request?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was trying to explain that he too had had victims in that war, but Mladic interrupted him. Mladic wouldn't let anyone discuss, and I had the feeling that he wanted to have the main say in the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody else have any say in the meeting or was General Mladic the person who was conducting the meeting alone?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was General Mladic who conducted the meeting alone most of the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me show you the next exhibit, which I'd ask also to be placed on the ELMO, which is Prosecutor's Exhibit 53. I'd also ask that that be disseminated to the Court and to counsel. This also, Mrs. Omanovic, is a still photograph, an image taken from the film we just saw. Do you recognise anybody in this particular image other than General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this man here [indicates].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're pointing to the man with the green shirt, civilian shirt, on the left-hand side of the image. How do you know that man?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm pointing at him. I just know him. I don't know what his name is. We used to run into each other in town. He lived in Bratunac, and I would often go to Bratunac to visit my sister. Bratunac was the town that was closest to Srebrenica, and we used to meet each other. We used to know a lot of people from Bratunac. And I went there, when I went to see about the situation, about the evacuation, I saw that man. He was standing somewhere near the buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he say, if anything?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said, "Mrs. Camila, where are your children?" But I lied to him. I told him that my children had already left by bus. He said, "No one can help you. Your fate has been determined." At that moment, I simply knew that nothing would go well, that we didn't have many chances of survival, myself and my family, because my children were still in front of the transport company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Omanovic, after the meeting concluded, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were taken back to the UN base. As we were going out, as we were going towards the UN camp, I saw that the Serb soldiers had already mingled with our population. They were armed and they were walking around. So I asked the driver to take me back to the location where my children were and he did that. So instead of going to the UN base, I went to my children. I was waiting for Nuhanovic and Mandzic to join us, because we had an agreement in Bratunac that there was supposed to be a list and the evacuation was supposed to begin with elderly people, women and children, and I thought that this would happen, but they never showed up. They never came back to do that. We simply saw trucks and buses arrive after that and there was no order whatsoever. People started boarding buses and the evacuation started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, on the 12th, did you also see General Mladic in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He was standing behind the yellow ribbon and he was accompanied by his soldiers. They distributed several bars of chocolate to the people who were standing next to that yellow ribbon. They walked around a little amongst the people who had been amassed there, and then after that he simply left somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said that people started to go toward the buses. Did that include families with male members, with fathers and sons?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of the families started boarding those trucks, and again there was a big crowd of people and the atmosphere was the same as the one in Srebrenica before that. People felt that they would be saved if they boarded trucks. Everybody was yelling. Children were crying. Everybody at the same time started moving towards the entrance where the buses were. Everybody together, including women and men and children.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anything happen to the men and the boys who were with the families moving toward the buses?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. They were being separated. Between buses and along the street where the buses were lined up for transport, there were lots of soldiers and civilians who had the right to separate people. It seemed that everybody had the right to separate people from the line. We didn't know the reason. We didn't know why. They were simply singling out people whom they didn't like, but I couldn't conclude anything as to the basis for that separation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, where did the men and the boys who were separated go?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went towards the White House. It was an uninterrupted column of people, very quiet, very calm, and you had the feeling that it would never stop, it would never be interrupted. New people were coming, and the people at the end of the column would disappear behind the White House.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges the range of ages of these males who had been separated and were queuing up in front of the White House?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them were above 13 years of age. There were lots of young boys who looked older, but those who were above 13 were separated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anybody -- any boy who happened to be disabled amongst the males who had been separated?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Mirza Mehmedovic. He was a totally handicapped person. He couldn't communicate at all. He was mentally retarded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he in line as well, going toward the White House?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He was trying to say something to them, but they simply pushed him aside. He was also separated, together with others. He was completely mentally retarded. He was unable to explain anything to anyone, but he was still separated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Omanovic, do you know if he survived?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not survive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the men who had been separated, did they have with them personal effects, bags of their possessions?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had their personal effects, but they couldn't take them into the White House. There was a huge pile of things and people were told to leave their personal belongings on that pile, that they couldn't take anything with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after you saw this, Mrs. Omanovic, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went back to my family, and at that point -- you mean after Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you had seen the separation of these men and boys and you'd seen General Mladic in and around Potocari, did you return back to the Zinc Factory and did you move to another location?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to the Zinc Factory where my family was, and I noticed there and all around the camp a number of armed people walking around. Next to my family, there were between five and ten soldiers standing. They were looking at my daughter and cursing, and I was really afraid to spend the night there. There was a little wood not far from there, and I was afraid that me, my daughter, my son, and the grandchild would be taken there. So I crossed over to the other side of the street, and we stood on a little clearing next to some buses. We put a blanket down and we sat there. There were lots of people around us. The transport was going on, but there was a number of people who were standing actually near where we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say that the soldiers were cursing, were they cursing at your daughter or were they cursing at other refugees?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were cursing my daughter. They were really very vulgar. "You're so young and you have a child." And it's true, she was very young, she had a child, but they were glancing at her with hostility, and I was really afraid for her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say you moved. Did you move to the bus compound across the way from the Zinc Factory?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is where I moved and this is where we stayed, on the following day as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how many other refugees were in and around the bus compound where you had relocated yourself?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody except for those who were not able to board the buses. Everybody was there and the space was getting narrower. We were crowded next to each other so as to be as close as possible to the transport, to the buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to estimate the number of people in and around the bus compound?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, it must have been several thousand, because in the evening, we learned that only 1.000 people had been able to leave. So everybody who eventually went to Tuzla was there, but we were all very crowded because people were in a hurry to board the buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to describe what you saw and what you heard the night of the 12th and the early morning of the 13th while you were at the bus compound.

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second night was even worse than the first night, and I think it was the worst night I ever had in my life. In the evening and throughout the night, Serb soldiers and Serb population were moving around on buses and trucks, and they were shouting, they were firing, they were going to Srebrenica and back. The Serbian soldiers would come to us with flashlights. They were singling out people, individuals, taking them away, and we would hear screams coming from behind the buses. A woman was giving birth. She was screaming. She had no one to help her. Another one was going completely crazy. This influenced other people as well and, in fact, the atmosphere in general. So we would move all of a sudden in waves, and then shortly after that we would be calm again. Then they threw some kind of sand on all of us and people started coughing. So people said that those were some kind of poisonous gases. We put the child in the pram and we covered the pram with something so as to help the baby. People were throwing up. But the night was very, very calm and some people started falling asleep. But from a nearby slaughterhouse, we all of a sudden heard a voice of a man who resembled the voice of Fikret Hodzic, whom we all knew very well, and it sounded as if he was being tortured. He would cry, "Nesib, Nesib." Then everybody else would start crying and yelling, and then everything would stop again. We didn't have enough -- we didn't have time to fall asleep or to keep quiet because screams would start all over again. It was a night of horror. And I was just trying to figure out how to save my children. I was not interested in living anymore. I just wanted to save my children. I wanted to cut my daughter's hair and to put a scarf on her head and to take her child away to try and make it on her own. I was talking to my son. But there was a man next to us. He was laying unconscious. He looked paralysed. And I told my son, "Go and sit by that man. Try to think of a fake name. Tell the people that this man is your grandfather, that you have to help him." But my son just simply sat next to me and he wouldn't listen to me. He didn't want to do that. And I spent all the night thinking how to save my children. And I moved towards the entrance where everybody else was. I really don't know how I was able to muster all that courage, because at the same time I witnessed this terrible scene of separation of people. They took their rucksacks and I took the baby. We put some food -- we took some food for the children and we grabbed each other. We took each other's hands and we were trying to make our way through the crowd. I no longer had any force left. I could not fight what was happening to me. So we came close to that white ribbon -- I'm sorry, yellow ribbon, yellow tape, where UNPROFOR buses were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there for just a minute. I'm sorry. But when you said -- I'd like to stay focused, if we can, for just a few more minutes, on the night before you attempted to board the buses yourself. So if we could stay focused on that for just a minute. You said that people would come into the compound and they would take refugees out of the compound. Who were those people who were coming into the compound and how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb soldiers came. They were wearing Serbian uniforms and UN uniforms, and they mingled with the population. They were walking amongst us and they were looking for people -- on what basis, I don't know -- using flashlights, and they would point to certain individuals, who would then be taken away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know a man by the name of Sefik Mustafic?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know him. He's a neighbour of mine. He was sitting next to us all that time while we were in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Judges what happened to that gentleman.

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sefic Mustafic was taken away, and after a while he returned. He was frightened. And we wanted to know what had happened, where he had been. But he said he didn't dare tell us everything, that he couldn't tell us everything, that perhaps one day he would tell us what had happened. So he spent some time sitting next to us and then he left. We thought he had just gone for a walk, but he hanged himself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you if while you were in the compound you had heard women being raped by Serb soldiers.

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything that took place in the camp we could see or hear, because we were sitting next to each other. Rumours were spreading quickly. We could hear about rapes, murders, people being taken away. We were all in the know, because we were all amassed at one place and news would spread quickly. So whoever saw something would tell it to his neighbours, so we knew exactly what was happening where in the camp, at all times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what effect did the separation of males, boys and husbands, from their families, what effect did the rumours of rapes, what effect did the cries of torture that you could hear in and around the bus compound have on the refugees who were in the bus compound?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the while while we were staying there in the camp, we were just trying to figure out who would be next to be killed or to be taken away. We were just waiting for that to happen. And that's why people were in such a hurry. That's why people wanted to leave as quickly as possible. People were losing patience. They wanted something to happen. They couldn't handle the uncertainty. And that was the effect on the population. We simply wanted to get away from there as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you subsequently learn that your young son had seen something while you were at the bus compound, and can you explain that to the Judges, please.

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My son went to fetch some water, and he saw five or six human bodies that had been slaughtered near the river bank. He wouldn't leave me after that. He didn't talk about it anymore, but he wouldn't be separated from me after he had seen that terrible scene.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Omanovic, I'd like to turn now to the morning of the 13th of July. Did you attempt to leave? Did you attempt to get on a bus or a truck? And can you explain to the Judges what happened?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that morning, I decided to leave. I took my children. We were holding each other's hands. I took the baby and I went to the -- up to the yellow ribbon. It was very difficult. Everybody was trying to leave. So I went to a vehicle which was a personnel carrier. I thought it was an ICRC vehicle. A lady was there who was acting as an interpreter. She was telling people to calm down. I tried to contact her. I tried to ask her to take the children and that I would come back, but she obviously didn't understand what I was saying. So I went to the first vehicle, but some people were standing there who wouldn't let us on, and we were not allowed to board any of those buses. But there were a lot of people behind us. Again, a separation was taking place. Some people were let on those buses, some were put aside. We were taken to the first truck, and near each truck there would be some kind of rock, or a stool, with some -- there was some jewellery on it. And one person asked -- one person gave me several rings and a medal, and I didn't know -- I couldn't figure out why he was doing so. And so he said, "You might need it in Bratunac." But we were afraid, because there were rumours that on the way to Bratunac, or where people -- where people would reach the Bosniak territory, that they were also being separated and their belongings were taken away from them. I started shouting, "Help, help." I thought it was the ICRC. I thought they would help us. And then the Serb soldiers said, "Just start the engine and leave." I had my two children on my sides and my daughter said, "Please, mother, don't cry. Let us just throw away this jewellery. No one will know that we had thrown it away." My children stayed on the truck and I jumped out of the truck, so they left in the direction of Bratunac. And there was an armed Serb soldier coming towards me, and he stopped me and he told me, "You will now see what's going to happen in Bratunac." And I told him, "Just kill me. I don't care about my life. Just leave my children alone." I managed to run away, and I went up to the barbed wire, which was very high. I couldn't jump over it, but there was a hole underneath, and I crawled through that hole and I managed to reach the UN base.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Omanovic, let me ask you: You mentioned Bratunac. Had something happened in Bratunac in 1992 or 1993 that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, people were separated in Bratunac. It was at the very beginning of the war. This took place on the Bratunac playground. Lots of people had been taken away on that occasion, and we haven't heard of them ever since, and they must have been killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after you crawled under the fence that you just described, what happened, Mrs. Omanovic?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I ran to the UN base and I called the interpreters. I told them that people should be helped and I told them that people were being taken off the buses on the way to Bratunac. And I told them that people were being separated elsewhere, not only in Potocari, and something should be done to help them. Then a brother of mine -- my brother came and I asked him to try to help me kill myself. I was afraid of falling into the hands of Serbian soldiers, because there were terrible stories that were being told about them. And at that moment I could only think of those rumours, those stories. There were stories about rapes, slaughters, and I was afraid that my daughter would be raped in front of my own eyes, that my grandchild would be slaughtered, and I couldn't simply face it. And this man, he had already prepared a rope --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but it's very difficult to follow the witness. The interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Omanovic, would you just slow down a bit? I've received a word from the interpretation booth that they're having difficulty because of the pace of your testimony. Could you slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. And my brother showed me the noose he had prepared for himself, and I pulled it out of his hand and I climbed to the upper floor of the UN base. There were lots of people, and children were standing at the window and watching those trucks moving away. And I asked them to go away from the window, because it was -- I had heard that a body of a person who hangs himself is very ugly. So that is what I tried to do. I climbed a chair and I saw two Serb soldiers with UN soldiers coming up, and I felt -- I must have been so terrified that I thought they were looking for me. So I climbed up on that rack which was there for drying and I laid there, and they walked up and down, were looking what was going on. They went around, they went back. And as they were climbing down the stairs I sat on that drying rack, on top of that drying rack, and I tightened the noose which I had already prepared, I put it around my neck, and I jumped down. And I woke up in the hospital and I really don't know what happened next.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Omanovic, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I've concluded my direct examination, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Before we move on to cross-examination, perhaps it would be good to make a break, so that now a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Omanovic, you will now be answering questions which the Defence counsel for General Krstic, that is, Mr. Petrusic or Mr. Visnjic, will ask you. Mr. Petrusic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours; good morning, my learned friends from the Prosecution. Cross-examined by Mr. Petrusic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Omanovic. Before I ask you some questions, I should like to tell you that it is not our intention to take you back to that period of July 1995 and all that you went through. We do not wish to revive all those memories. We hope that as an educated woman and emancipated woman, you will understand that the principal objective of the defence is the establishment of the truth and all that happened in Srebrenica, and that is all we have in mind. Now I should like to move on to some specific questions. Mrs. Omanovic, at the beginning of your testimony, you said that on the 10th of July, men were separated from the rest of the Muslim population, next to the petrol station in Srebrenica. Could you please tell us if that separation was spontaneous or did somebody invite people to split into two groups?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could say that it was spontaneous. As they came out of the town, men and women headed for Potocari and men towards Kazani, and, yes, it was next to the petrol station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among the men, were there some wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know when I should begin to answer. If I could know only when to start answering. If somebody could tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we seem to have the problem with the language because we speak the same language.

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Somebody told me --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, at the end of each of my questions, should I say, "This is the end of my question," so that the witness knows that she can begin with her answer? Could I do that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon perhaps will explain. Yes, Mr. Petrusic. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I explained to the witness, because counsel speaks the same language as the witness, that she needed to pause so that we didn't have overlap and create a problem for the interpreters, and I think that is the source of the problem. She is inquiring when she needs to commence her answer. So that, I think, is the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. Harmon, very much for this clarification. Mr. Petrusic, Mrs. Omanovic, as you know, when we speak the same language, then there is always a risk of speaking too fast and not making a pause so the interpreters can keep up, because the interpreters are always a couple of seconds behind of what was being said. So could you just wait a little. So Mr. Petrusic, if you just make a pause after you finish your question. When you hear the end of Mr. Petrusic's questions, just make a short pause. I believe you understand really when the question has ended. You do not have to hear, "This is the end of the question." Just wait for a while after you've heard the question to give the interpreters time. Simply remember that there's always one person between you, which is an interpreter. So I believe that -- of course, Mr. Petrusic, you can also do as you suggested, "This is the end of my question," but do I not think there is any need for this. I'm quite sure that we shall have a very good communication even without that if you only make this short pause. Yes, Mr. Petrusic, move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mrs. Omanovic, would you please answer my questions. Among those men, were there any wearing uniforms?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were some uniformed men. Not very many, but here and there. Some of them had weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They formed a column, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, they didn't form a column. All I could see was only the beginning. Whether they formed a column further on, I wouldn't know. But from the street, men simply separated and they came together in groups. There were groups like ours, except they were groups of men on that other side, but they were not columns.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Omanovic, I should like to move on to the meeting on the 12th of July, at the Fontana Hotel in Bratunac around 10.00. We saw the footage. Did General Mladic introduce each one of the participants in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. General Mladic did introduce all the participants of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As he introduced General Krstic, did he say anything about him?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember him saying anything. I was too frightened, and I can't recall quite a number of details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did General Krstic take an active role in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't remember him saying anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And any one of the other participants in the meeting, did he take part in the discussion?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Omanovic, could you tell us: What were the conclusions of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a rule that a meeting reaches some conclusions and that the record is made or something like that, but our meeting ended in a rather unusual way. Somebody came in and said that people had broken into the stadium, as if all this crowd had broken in, so that we stood up, simply. Nobody was taking minutes, nobody signed anything, nothing that should be a normal routine at a meeting, some items on the agenda or something. It was all incidental, that somebody needs to provide trucks, that somebody needs to take fuel or something, but there was nothing that would make it look like a proper meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you know if some minutes were made later on, or a record? Was it made later on?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know when a woman -- I don't know what her name was -- some foreign television crew arrived to make an interview with me to shoot something, and then somebody -- his name was Mila. He was an interpreter. I believe he was a Slovenian. He showed me something which was supposedly the record of that meeting, and it figured my -- made a name, but it was not my signature. So that was the first thing that I saw as a can kind of a record of that meeting, but I did not see anyone taking it during the meeting or anyone preparing it for signature when the meeting ended. The meeting ended just out of the blue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after that meeting did you see General Mladic in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him when he arrived with a group of soldiers. He walked around the compound and he distributed some chocolates to the children. But I think he's a great actor and he was doing this only because there were some cameras shooting him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just for a moment, I should like to go back to the previous night, between the 11th and the 12th of July. Was there any gunfire around the compound then?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And between the 12th and the 13th, during that night?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Omanovic, in your testimony you said that you heard rumours about rapes. Was it anything more than rumours, or did it end there; that is, did you receive any more reliable, any more trustworthy information?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in my testimony that I did not see a single murder, I mean with my own eyes. I did not witness a rape. I heard all those sounds and everything, but I did not see it with my own eyes. But in that compound, in that place where we were, the rumour of any evil deed, of anything that happened, yes, spread around, but I did not witness any of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 13th of July, you and your family were not allowed to board the buses that were parked there, were you?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite right. They did not allow us. And I think that during this meeting with Mladic I did ask not to transport us as cattle, because I must again repeat what I'd heard: that so many babies suffocated in that crowd, the first group that was transported to Bratunac. And I asked him to treat us properly as human beings. And he knew that I had a baby of three months, and he said, "At some point I'll take you in my own bus." But he would not allow it. I wasn't asking for myself. He wouldn't allow my baby to board the bus, but the truck, and then they stoned the truck and did all sorts of things that they were not to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who, then, boarded those parked buses which were standing next to those trucks?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, people; again, the crowd -- I don't know how to explain it to you. Next to every bus there were standing men who were selecting. I don't know what method they used, because there are always some selection methods. Somebody says, "You can board," or "Just let him through." Or other people they wouldn't allow it, because there were very many men among those buses and were they simply selecting it. And they would simply put their shoulder, put their elbow out, and would simply prevent him from boarding the bus if they thought that that person shouldn't board the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those men who were making the selection who would and who would not board the bus, were they in uniforms?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some were uniformed and some were in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Omanovic, perhaps this is asking you to do too much, in view of the state that you must have been in at the time, but please allow me to ask you if perhaps you noticed the patches, the insignia, the flashes of the military or the police or some other units there. Do you have any recollection of that? Can you tell us something about it?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me that at that moment, whether I simply didn't want to or whether I didn't dare look at any man, but I cannot bring back to my mind any single face. I merely held my children next to me and I was trying to board it. Nobody, except that man who was at the meeting and who said that my fate was sealed, I did not recognise anyone. Was that fear? Was it something -- I don't know. But I wasn't really looking at any one of them in the face; I was simply trying to board as soon as possible, to get my children on board. No, nobody. Insignia, no. I simply didn't look at those men who were there. I knew they wouldn't allow me to board, but who and why, I don't not know. I simply cannot remember and I cannot bring back to my mind any of the flashes, any of the insignia, and I really don't know who that was or what they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Omanovic, thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I do not, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Judge Riad. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Mrs. Omanovic, good morning. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I don't want to prolong your difficult situation of testifying to these very sad events. I just would like to understand two more things. You mentioned that General Mladic reiterated that you have either to leave or perish. Leave what? What is the area which he meant by "to leave"; to leave the area of Srebrenica or to leave a bigger area? In your opinion, what was this area which he meant?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he meant the area of Srebrenica, because that is the only point not held by Serbs. We were encircled as if we were in a camp, because the whole territory, all the hills around my town were held by Serbs. And so if we left, then this whole territory would be Serb. Because in the Drina Canyon, we were from all sides surrounded by Serbs, and only that enclave, Srebrenica, was the territory which the Serbs had not captured yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But also you could not go to any other Serb part of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody. It was only -- I don't really know why, but nobody asked us, nobody made any lists, nobody talked to us to reach some understanding, or anything. They simply brought the buses. And they knew, because such chaos reigned in Srebrenica, so they knew if they brought those five buses, or any number of vehicles, that people were simply set off. Because before that, they had passed such horrible nights that each one of us wished to be dead. The ordinary death would have been a blessing for us, and we suffered so much. We simply wanted to get away, to get away, only not to stay there. And we didn't even have any other possibility. It was, I think, a mere formality. Nobody asked us anything. Those buses were brought there and people were crowded, and that is how the transport started. We had no say in the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good. You also mentioned more than once that -- I can almost repeat what you said: People would -- anybody could come to the compound and point out to any person, to any individual, to be taken away. What do you mean by, "Anybody could come and point out"? You meant soldiers, Bosnian Serb soldiers, or you meant even individuals, any Serb would come and choose a prey to take out?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were only Serb soldiers, Bosnian Serb soldiers. They were taking away with those torchlamps pointed at them. In daytime they would walk around people, among those crowds, and people were gathered there on two sides, and they would just walk among them and take away those men and never came back. They would take one man after another one. They would talk to him, walk with him, and then they would be gone. Then at night they would once again come, point their torches at those men and just call out individual men and none of those men came back again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned that among these people there were UN -- people with UN uniforms. Did I understand you rightly?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did. The second night, the Serb soldiers dressed -- because they spoke the same language, Bosnian, and they had UN uniforms, and they came wearing uniforms as they came to us and moved around us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So it was Serb soldiers wearing UN uniforms? I don't hear you.

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They were Serb soldiers wearing UN uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Riad. Judge Wald, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Just a few. When the people boarded the buses in Potocari, they were in a great rush to get on the buses and to get out of there, as you have told us. Did the people around you know where they were going? Did they know what would happen to them when they reached a certain place, or did they simply get on the buses just to get out of Potocari?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to put an end to this agony, people were leaving. They didn't know where they were leaving, but they just wanted to put an end to that. They didn't know whether they would survive or die. They didn't know where they were going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: You also mentioned that on one of the nights there were screams around the compound, but you could hear them but you didn't know what was actually happening. Were any of those screams women's screams?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were women's screams as well. There was a woman giving birth, which was not far from me. She was crying. There was another woman that simply went crazy on a bus. She was -- this was influencing us all. It affected the atmosphere and created the atmosphere of terror that night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: My last question is: You said that you feared very much falling into the hands of Serbian soldiers or having your daughter fall into their hands, and you referred to things that had happened on the buses on the way to Bratunac. How did you know what happened to any of the buses after they left Potocari? Where did that information come from that caused you fear that if you got on the buses some bad things might happen and made you go to the UN authorities and complain?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where those stories had come from, who was the origin of those rumours. All I know is that throughout that period which we spent in Srebrenica, terrible stories about genocide, for example, were being told, genocide perpetrated by Serbian soldiers on the civilian population, women, children. We were afraid of every single soldier. We saw monsters in all of them, monsters who were capable of most inhumane things. This is why I was so fearful to end up in their hands. Because death is nothing, but the way one dies is what counts, because we had been hearing table stories about Serbian soldiers torturing people, mutilating people, raping women, and I simply couldn't allow that to happen to my children, because I was, in a way, guilty for leaving them in Srebrenica, and I would have been responsible for their fate. I was the one who actually made that decision in Srebrenica. They were much too young to leave on their own. This is why I felt so terrible, this is why I jumped out. I just tried to see whether any help was possible. It's very difficult for me to be more precise. This is what we had heard, what we had been hearing all that time. Sometimes throughout that period we would either listen to the radio or saw a TV broadcast, but nothing that we saw on TV or heard on the radio was very nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: But your fears were generated by these stories of what had happened in other villages and elsewhere, but you didn't have any specific information about what had happened to the people on the bus that had left Potocari; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taking people away. They were taking them away from the camp. We could hear screams throughout the night. It was very difficult, because we felt that something terrible would happen. During that night we were just sitting there, and all of a sudden we would hear screams from a man who was being tortured. It's a terrible thing to experience. Because of such rumours, because of such stories, we all feared that we would be the next. Maybe it was only my imagination, I don't know, but if you keep hearing horrible stories, you cannot be assured that your life would be spared. When he said that he would take my children in a special vehicle, whereas we were actually not allowed to board the bus at all, and I knew that I couldn't expect anything good to happen to me in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Omanovic.

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Omanovic, I have at least four questions for you. My first question is the following: Whilst you were at the meeting with General Mladic, at one point he told you that you could choose between surviving and vanishing, and you said that "vanish" could, in a way, also include the possibility of survival somehow. What I would like to know is whether this possibility of survival was a conclusion of yours or was it General Mladic who had actually said that?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he simply said, "You can survive or vanish." My conclusion was that if I leave, I would be saved; and if I stayed, I would die.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. So the way you understood it was that there was actually no choice, because if you chose to stay, this would mean not to survive. Was that the case?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My second question: There were people who were at the meeting together with you, and there was someone who told you at that meeting that your fate had been sealed. How did you interpret that particular message?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought I would simply disappear. I thought that nobody could help me. I thought I had to be the one who had to vanish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you understood that something had already been prepared or determined in advance for you?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, because when he saw that my fate had been sealed and when we reached the buses, when we were not allowed to board the buses, when I got to that truck where I was given this medal, I knew that something was brewing, something bad. I had the typical instinct of a mother. I wasn't worried about myself. I felt sorry for my children. At that moment, I just jumped out. They said I was brave at that moment. No. No, I wasn't. I was just acting on the instinct of a mother who had to protect her children. That is why I jumped off the truck. I ran to that soldier who pointed his gun towards me and said to him, "Kill me, just leave my children alone. They're innocent. They're underage. My son is there on the truck." And this soldier was also frightened of me although he had a gun. But my instinct as a mother was much stronger, and I had enough force to run away. The UN base was not very close by. My children were leaving to an unknown destination. I didn't know what was going to happen to them, but I had enough force to fight because of this maternal instinct in me. I thought that there must be something that can be done to help my children who had been taken away. They were both under-aged. That's why I jumped out of that truck. I wasn't brave, I was just trying to use the little force that was left in me in order to save my children. I apologise for crying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please do calm down. We have profound respect for you and what you have suffered, and you are indeed a brave woman, because you needed a lot of force, a lot of strength to experience what you have been through. We also know you are a brave woman because you have come here to testify. May I continue, Mrs. Omanovic?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Omanovic, you described, in very negative terms, Serbian soldiers. I would like to know: What was their image before the war? Did they have this negative image before or was it only the result of the war?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just have a sip of water and I will tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please relax, Mrs. Omanovic.

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to the war, Serbian soldiers were not behaving that way, or maybe they were simply pretending. We lived together, we socialised with each other, we lived next to each other, we went to school together, we worked together, and we respected mutually our traditions, and it was very difficult to understand where all that hatred had come from on the part of the people who had lived together with us. When I think back, I know that I worked together with four Serbs and two Muslims when I was working as the chief accountant at that company. We lived together very well. We had a good life. We would visit each other. I would bake typical Muslim cakes for my Serbian friends for their family reunions and celebrations, and it was so strange to see such a sudden change. We couldn't realise where all that hatred had come from. Today, after all that has happened, I'm simply unable to understand the atrocities, how anyone could commit such atrocities. They knew we had problems because of the concentration of iodine in the factory and there was some very typical diseases for that area, but we never received any necessary medicine from them during that time. It was also a kind of -- it was a method to intimidate us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my fourth question, Mrs. Omanovic: We saw several videotapes, and we saw the confusion which reigned in and around the base. You lived through all that, and I would like to know whether amidst that turmoil -- you were an educated person -- did you manage to notice, were you able to observe any signs of organisation? Could you tell that things had been prepared in advance in any way?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have a feeling, because of what was going on, that we had been brought to a stage where everything had been prepared in advance, that there was a team of people working in an organised manner. And, for example, at that meeting, things happened in such a way that I had the impression that everything was organised, and then the meeting stopped abruptly, and that was very strange. So, well, this is the impression that I had at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who do you think was the chief organiser of all that?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was General Mladic. He was a kind of director there and he was also acting his role in that scene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have a fifth question, Mrs. Omanovic. You know who General Krstic is, don't you?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard a lot about General Krstic. I met him for the first time in Bratunac during the negotiations. However, I had never seen him before that meeting, nor did I see him after the meeting. I haven't seen him, actually, until I've come here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say that you met him for the first time at the meeting in Bratunac. How did you know that the person in question was General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe that introductions were made at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So somebody introduced you, introduced General Krstic to you. Do you remember the exact words that were used during that introduction?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, "This is General Krstic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just like that? Did they say anything about his function?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember where in the room, where the meeting was being held, did General Krstic sit?

utterances.speaker: CAMILA OMANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he was sitting on General Mladic's left-hand side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you. Mrs. Omanovic, thank you very much for your answers to both my questions and questions put to you by my colleagues. Mrs. Omanovic, you have completed your testimony here before the International Criminal Tribunal, and I should like to express our gratitude for your coming here. We do think you were a very brave person, despite what you may think of yourself. We can also tell that you're a tolerant person, reasonable person, and I hope that you yourself can also make a personal contribution so that your country may again find peace and safety. Once again, thank you very much, Mrs. Omanovic, for coming to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, I think we should perhaps start with your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I move into evidence exhibits that were introduced through this

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: is the film of the meeting on the 12th of July; Prosecutor's Exhibit 49A, B, and C, which are transcripts of the meeting; Prosecutor's Exhibit 50, which is a video, the first video which I played showing the people, the refugees; Prosecutor's 51, which is a 48-second video showing crowd scenes; Prosecutor's 52, which is a still photograph taken from the video; and Prosecutor's 53, likewise a still photograph taken from Prosecutor's Exhibit 49.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. The exhibits have been admitted into evidence. Mr. Harmon, perhaps we can begin the testimony of your next witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm informed by my colleague, Mr. Cayley, that this witness will require a closed session, and we're prepared to proceed with the next witness once the courtroom is closed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm addressing the public now. We are now going to move into closed session for our following witness. However, before we do so, I have to ask Mr. Petrusic whether he has any objections against protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have reached an agreement, Your Honour, and we do not have any objections to protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. Let us prepare the courtroom for the closed session, during which we will hear our following witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: at 2.36 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 24th day of March, 2000, at 9.30 a.m.
